title: Job postings on Indeed
description: Daily count of U.S. job postings on Indeed relative to before the pandemic, seasonally adjusted.

source.dataset: Job Postings Tracker (aggregate, U.S.)

howToRead: Above 100 means more postings than just before the pandemic; below 100 means fewer.
caveats: Postings on one website, not total U.S. job openings. The official measure is the BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS).

source.dataset: Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE)

howToRead: Model-based single-year estimates that combine survey data with tax and program records, so even small counties get a yearly number.
title: Median household income by county
description: Income of the household in the middle of each county.
caveats: Not adjusted for inflation between years, or for local cost of living.
Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.

title: Median household income by state
description: Income of the household in the middle of each state's distribution, adjusted for inflation by the Census Bureau.

source.dataset: Current Population Survey, Annual Social and Economic Supplement
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Median means half of households earn more and half earn less, so a few very high earners do not skew it.
caveats: State estimates come from a survey sample and have wide margins of error; differences of a few thousand dollars between states are often not meaningful.
Not adjusted for cost of living, which varies a lot between states.

title: Minimum wage by state
description: The minimum hourly wage set by each state's law.

source.dataset: State Minimum Wage Rates
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Where a state's minimum is below $7.25 or it has none, the federal minimum of $7.25 applies to most workers.
Many cities and counties set higher local minimums.
caveats: States with no minimum wage law of their own show as no data.
Nominal dollars, not adjusted for inflation.

title: New business applications by state
description: Applications for a new employer ID number (EIN) each month, a leading sign of new businesses, per 100,000 residents.

source.dataset: Business Formation Statistics (seasonally adjusted)

howToRead: An application is an intention to start a business; only some become employers. Applications jumped in mid-2020 and stayed high.
caveats: Per-person rate computed by Civic Charts with Census population estimates.

title: Personal income per person by state
description: All income received by a state's residents (wages, benefits, investment income) divided by its population.

source.dataset: State Annual Personal Income (SAINC)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: An average, so high earners pull it up. Median household income better describes a typical family.
caveats: In current dollars, not adjusted for inflation or cost of living.

source.dataset: Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE)

howToRead: Model-based single-year estimates that combine survey data with tax and program records, so even small counties get a yearly number.
title: Poverty rate by county
description: Share of people whose family income is below the federal poverty threshold.
caveats: Each county estimate has a margin of error; for small counties the 90% range is often several points wide, so close rankings are not meaningful.
Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.

title: U.S. consumer sentiment
description: How Americans feel about their finances and the economy, from a monthly survey.

source.dataset: Surveys of Consumers, Index of Consumer Sentiment
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Measures feelings, not spending. Sentiment and actual spending often move apart.
caveats: Survey of roughly 600-1,000 people a month; moves of 2-3 points can be noise.
The survey changed from phone to online interviews in 2024, which may affect comparisons with earlier years.

title: U.S. inflation rate
description: How much consumer prices rose compared with the same month a year earlier (CPI-U, seasonally adjusted).

source.dataset: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: This is the rate prices are rising, not the price level. Falling inflation means prices are rising more slowly, not that they are falling.
"Core" inflation removes food and energy, which swing a lot month to month.
caveats: CPI tracks a basket of goods for urban consumers; individual households can experience very different inflation.

title: U.S. unemployment rate
description: Share of the labor force that is jobless and actively looking for work, seasonally adjusted.

source.dataset: Current Population Survey (LNS14000000)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: The headline rate (U-3) only counts people actively searching for work in the past four weeks.
U-6 adds discouraged workers and part-timers who want full-time work, so it always runs higher.
caveats: People who stop looking for work leave the labor force and are not counted as unemployed, which can push the headline rate down even when the job market is weak.

title: Unemployment rate by state
description: Seasonally adjusted unemployment rate for each state and D.C.

source.dataset: Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: State rates are modeled estimates and are revised every year in March.
caveats: Small states have larger margins of error; month-to-month moves of a few tenths of a point are often noise.

source.dataset: County Presidential Election Returns 2000-2024 (official results from state election offices)

howToRead: Margin = Democratic share minus Republican share of all votes cast. +10 means the Democratic candidate led by 10 points; −10 means the Republican candidate did.
Third-party and write-in votes count toward the total, so the two shares add to less than 100%.
title: Presidential election results by county
description: How each county voted for president, 2000 to 2024, as the margin between the Democratic and Republican candidates.
caveats: A shaded map gives large, empty counties the same weight as big cities. The votes-cast fact and the bar view show where the voters are.
Alaska reports results by state house district, not county, so it shows as no data.
Certified results compiled by MIT Election Data + Science Lab; small differences from a state's own canvass are possible.

source.dataset: County Presidential Election Returns 2000-2024 (official results from state election offices)

howToRead: Margin = Democratic share minus Republican share of all votes cast. +10 means the Democratic candidate led by 10 points; −10 means the Republican candidate did.
Third-party and write-in votes count toward the total, so the two shares add to less than 100%.
title: Presidential election results by state
description: Statewide margin between the Democratic and Republican presidential candidates, 2000 to 2024.
caveats: The national popular vote and the Electoral College can differ: the winner of the most votes nationally lost the presidency in 2000 and 2016.
Certified results compiled by MIT Election Data + Science Lab.

source.dataset: Weekly Retail Gasoline Prices, Regular, All Formulations
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: National average of regular gasoline prices, including taxes.
title: U.S. gas price
description: Average retail price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S.
caveats: Prices are in dollars of each year. A $3 gallon in 2008 cost more in today's money than a $3 gallon today.

source.dataset: Weekly Retail Gasoline Prices, Regular, All Formulations
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: National average of regular gasoline prices, including taxes.
title: U.S. gas price, adjusted for inflation
description: Average retail price of regular gasoline, converted into today's dollars using CPI-U.
caveats: Adjusted with the all-items CPI computed by Civic Charts; the source publishes nominal prices only.

title: Days with unhealthy air by county
description: Days each year when the Air Quality Index was unhealthy for sensitive groups or worse.

source.dataset: Air Quality System, annual AQI by county

howToRead: Above 100 on the Air Quality Index, children, older adults and people with heart or lung disease should limit time outdoors.
Wildfire smoke drives many of the worst recent years in the West.
caveats: Only counties with air monitors appear, and only years with at least 120 monitored days. Most rural counties have no monitor, which is not the same as clean air.
Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.

title: Earthquakes in the past 30 days
description: Every earthquake of magnitude 2.5 or greater recorded worldwide in the last 30 days.

source.dataset: Earthquake Hazards Program real-time feed (M2.5+, past 30 days)

howToRead: Magnitude is logarithmic: each whole number up releases about 32 times more energy.
caveats: Small quakes are detected far more often near dense sensor networks (like the U.S.), so the map over-represents those regions at low magnitudes.

title: Federal disaster declarations by county since 1965

source.dataset: OpenFEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries (v2)

description: How many major disaster declarations have covered each county, adding up year by year.
howToRead: Watch it fill in: the coasts, Tornado Alley and river valleys light up first.
caveats: A declaration is a federal funding decision, not a direct measure of how severe a disaster was. Thresholds and politics change over time.
COVID-19 declarations (2020) are left out because they covered every state at once.
Statewide declarations without county detail are not counted.
Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.

title: Global temperature
description: Global average surface temperature over land and ocean compared with the 1951-1980 average.

source.publisher: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies
source.dataset: GISTEMP v4, Land-Ocean Temperature Index

howToRead: Zero is the 1951-1980 average, not "normal" in any deeper sense. The change over time is what matters.
Single months are noisy (El Niño years run hot); the annual average shows the trend.
caveats: Recent months are revised slightly as late station reports arrive.

title: Heat wave risk by county

source.dataset: National Risk Index for Natural Hazards (counties)

howToRead: Scores run from 0 to 100 and rank each county against all others: 90 means riskier than 90% of U.S. counties. It is not a probability.
Risk combines how often a hazard strikes, what is in harm's way, how vulnerable people are and how well communities can recover.
caveats: A model built by FEMA from historical hazard data; it is updated every year or two.
Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.

source.dataset: National Risk Index for Natural Hazards (counties)

howToRead: Scores run from 0 to 100 and rank each county against all others: 90 means riskier than 90% of U.S. counties. It is not a probability.
Risk combines how often a hazard strikes, what is in harm's way, how vulnerable people are and how well communities can recover.
caveats: A model built by FEMA from historical hazard data; it is updated every year or two.

source.dataset: OpenFEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries (v2)

howToRead: Each declaration unlocks federal aid for a state or tribe after a disaster that overwhelms local resources.
caveats: A declaration is a federal funding decision, not a direct measure of how severe a disaster was. Thresholds and politics change over time.
COVID-19 declarations (2020) are left out because they covered every state at once.

source.dataset: National Risk Index for Natural Hazards (counties)

Risk combines how often a hazard strikes, what is in harm's way, how vulnerable people are and how well communities can recover.
caveats: A model built by FEMA from historical hazard data; it is updated every year or two.

title: Federal revenue vs. spending
description: Total federal receipts and total federal outlays, each as a share of GDP. The gap between them is the deficit.

source.publisher: U.S. Office of Management and Budget
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
source.dataset: Federal Receipts (FYFRGDA188S) and Outlays (FYONGDA188S) as Percent of GDP

howToRead: When the spending line is above the revenue line, the government ran a deficit that year; the distance between them is its size.
Fiscal years run October through September and are named for the year they end: FY2026 is Oct 2025 to Sep 2026.
caveats: Revenue falls and spending rises automatically in recessions (lower tax receipts, more unemployment benefits), so gaps widen in downturns regardless of policy.

title: Interest on the national debt
description: What the federal government pays in interest on its debt, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate.

source.dataset: Federal government current expenditures: Interest payments (A091RC1Q027SBEA)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Quarterly figures are expressed as a yearly pace, so each point is roughly what a full year would cost at that rate.
Interest grows when the debt grows and when the rates the Treasury pays on new borrowing rise.
caveats: National-accounts measure from BEA; Treasury budget figures for net interest differ somewhat in definition and timing.
In dollars of each year; the share-of-GDP view adjusts for the size of the economy.

title: Interest on the national debt as a share of GDP

unit.label: Net interest outlays as % of GDP

description: Federal net interest outlays divided by GDP, by fiscal year.

source.publisher: U.S. Office of Management and Budget
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
source.dataset: Federal Outlays: Interest as Percent of GDP (FYOIGDA188S)

howToRead: Shows how much of the economy goes to paying interest on federal debt.
Fiscal years run October through September and are named for the year they end: FY2026 is Oct 2025 to Sep 2026.
caveats: Updated once a year, after the fiscal year closes.

title: U.S. federal budget deficit
description: Federal surplus or deficit for each fiscal year: total receipts minus total outlays.

source.publisher: U.S. Office of Management and Budget
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
source.dataset: Federal Surplus or Deficit (FYFSD)

howToRead: Below zero is a deficit (the government spent more than it collected); above zero is a surplus.
Fiscal years run October through September and are named for the year they end: FY2026 is Oct 2025 to Sep 2026.
The deficit is one year of borrowing; the national debt is the running total of past deficits (plus other borrowing).
caveats: In dollars of each year, so recent deficits look larger partly because prices and the economy are bigger. The share-of-GDP view corrects for that.

title: U.S. federal budget deficit as a share of GDP

unit.label: Surplus or deficit (-) as % of GDP

description: Federal surplus or deficit divided by the size of the economy, by fiscal year.

source.publisher: U.S. Office of Management and Budget
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
source.dataset: Federal Surplus or Deficit as Percent of GDP (FYFSGDA188S)

howToRead: Below zero is a deficit (the government spent more than it collected); above zero is a surplus.
Fiscal years run October through September and are named for the year they end: FY2026 is Oct 2025 to Sep 2026.
This is how economists compare deficits across decades: a $1 trillion deficit means far less in a $30 trillion economy than in a $10 trillion one.
caveats: Updated once a year, after the fiscal year closes and GDP for it is estimated, so it lags the dollar figures.

title: U.S. federal budget deficit, last 12 months
description: Federal surplus or deficit over the 12 months ending each month, from the Monthly Treasury Statement.

source.dataset: Monthly Treasury Statement, Federal Surplus or Deficit (MTSDS133FMS), 12-month sum computed by Civic Charts
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Below zero is a deficit (the government spent more than it collected); above zero is a surplus.
Each point adds up the latest 12 months, so it updates monthly without the big swings single months show around tax deadlines.
The deficit is one year of borrowing; the national debt is the running total of past deficits (plus other borrowing).
caveats: Shifts in payment timing (when a due date falls on a weekend) can move a month between fiscal years and nudge the 12-month total.

title: U.S. national debt
description: Total public debt outstanding of the U.S. government, end of each month.

source.dataset: Debt to the Penny

howToRead: Includes debt held by the public and money the government owes to its own trust funds (like Social Security).
caveats: A growing economy and inflation make nominal debt rise almost every year. Debt as a share of GDP is the measure economists use to judge whether it is getting harder to carry.

title: U.S. national debt as a share of GDP
description: Total public debt divided by the size of the U.S. economy (gross domestic product).

source.publisher: U.S. Office of Management and Budget
source.dataset: Total Public Debt as Percent of GDP (GFDEGDQ188S)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Above 100% means the debt is larger than one full year of everything the U.S. economy produces.
caveats: GDP collapsed briefly in 2020, which spiked the ratio even before new borrowing showed up.

title: U.S. national debt, adjusted for inflation
description: Total public debt converted into today's dollars with CPI-U.

source.dataset: Debt to the Penny, deflated by BLS CPI-U

howToRead: Removes the effect of rising prices so years can be compared directly.
caveats: Inflation adjustment computed by Civic Charts with CPI-U.

title: Adult obesity by county
description: Adults with obesity (BMI 30+), age-adjusted, as estimated by the CDC for every county.

source.dataset: PLACES: Local Data for Better Health, County Data

howToRead: Age-adjusted, so counties with older or younger populations can be compared fairly.
caveats: These are model-based estimates from a national survey (BRFSS) combined with Census data, not direct counts for each county. Small differences between neighboring counties are not meaningful.
Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.

source.dataset: VSRR Provisional Drug Overdose Death Counts

howToRead: Each year is the 12 months ending in December, by the state where the death occurred.
title: Drug overdose death rate by state
description: Reported drug overdose deaths per 100,000 residents, 12 months ending in December.
caveats: Rate computed by Civic Charts using Census population estimates. It is not age-adjusted, unlike CDC's official rates.
Recent months are provisional and are usually revised upward.

source.publisher: CDC National Center for Health Statistics
source.dataset: VSRR Provisional Drug Overdose Death Counts

howToRead: Each year is the 12 months ending in December, by the state where the death occurred.
title: Drug overdose deaths by state
description: Reported drug overdose deaths in each state for the 12 months ending in December.
caveats: Totals mostly track population size. Compare states using the per-100,000 rate instead.
Recent months are provisional and are usually revised upward.

title: Drug recalls
description: Drug recalls reported to the FDA each month, by how serious the risk is.

source.dataset: openFDA drug enforcement reports

howToRead: Class I: reasonable chance of serious harm or death. Class II: temporary or reversible harm. Class III: unlikely to cause harm.
One recall can cover many products and lots, so counts measure recall actions, not the amount of product.
caveats: openFDA notes its data is not validated for medical decisions. Months reflect when FDA published the report, not when the problem started.

title: Food recalls

title: 30-year mortgage rate
description: Average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S., surveyed weekly.

source.dataset: Primary Mortgage Market Survey
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Rates are averages for borrowers with strong credit and 20% down; most people are quoted something different.
caveats: A lower rate does not always mean cheaper housing; home prices often rise when rates fall.

title: Home price growth by state
description: How much home prices have grown in each state since 1980, from repeat sales of the same houses.

source.dataset: All-Transactions House Price Index
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: Each state starts at 100 in 1980, so 500 means prices are five times their 1980 level. It compares growth, not price levels: a state at 400 is not more expensive than one at 300.
caveats: Not adjusted for inflation.

source.dataset: Median Sales Price of Houses Sold for the United States (MSPUS)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: This is the median price of newly built single-family homes sold, not all homes.
title: Median price of new U.S. homes
description: Median sales price of new houses sold in the United States.
caveats: Not adjusted for inflation, and the mix of homes being built changes over time (bigger homes push the median up).

source.dataset: Median Sales Price of Houses Sold for the United States (MSPUS)
source.via: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

howToRead: This is the median price of newly built single-family homes sold, not all homes.
title: Median price of new U.S. homes, adjusted for inflation
description: Median sales price of new houses converted into today's dollars with CPI-U.
caveats: Inflation adjustment computed by Civic Charts using CPI-U.

source.dataset: Building Permits Survey, annual state totals

howToRead: Permits are the earliest sign of new housing: most permitted homes are started within a few months.
caveats: Counts new privately owned units in permit-issuing places, which cover nearly all construction. The latest year can be revised.
title: New homes permitted by state
description: New housing units authorized by building permits each year.

source.dataset: Building Permits Survey, annual state totals

title: New homes permitted per 1,000 residents
description: New housing units authorized by building permits each year, per 1,000 residents.

title: Typical home value by state
description: Zillow's estimate of the typical value of homes in each state (the middle third of the market), seasonally adjusted.

source.dataset: Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI), all homes, mid-tier

howToRead: This is a model estimate of what homes are worth, including homes that did not sell, not a record of sale prices.
caveats: Not adjusted for inflation.

description: Natural change: births minus deaths each year, per 1,000 residents. Below zero means deaths outnumbered births.
howToRead: Older counties, especially rural ones, often have more deaths than births even before anyone moves away.

source.dataset: County Population Totals and Components of Change, Vintage 2025

source.dataset: County Population by Characteristics (age and sex), Vintage 2025

howToRead: Percent change from the April 2020 Census base, so small counties can swing a lot from a few hundred people.

source.dataset: County Population by Characteristics (age and sex), Vintage 2025

source.dataset: County Population Totals, Vintage 2025

title: Where Americans are moving, by county
description: People moving into a county from elsewhere in the U.S., minus people moving out, per 1,000 residents.
howToRead: Positive means more people arrived from other parts of the U.S. than left. Immigration from abroad is counted separately and is not included.
caveats: Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.

title: Homicide rate by state
description: Murder and nonnegligent manslaughter reported to police, per 100,000 residents.

source.dataset: Crime Data Explorer, Uniform Crime Reporting (summarized)

howToRead: Counts crimes reported to police, not all crimes: many go unreported, especially property crimes and rape.
The FBI changed reporting systems in 2021 and many agencies did not submit that year, so 2021 is the least complete year.
caveats: A state-year is left blank when agencies covering less than 60% of its residents reported (78 blanks).

Rates are computed from the agencies that reported. The FBI's official national estimates fill in for non-reporting agencies and run 1-6% lower in some years (1991: about 758 violent crimes per 100,000 vs. 798 here). Cite "FBI Crime Data Explorer, reported agencies" when using these.
Definitions changed over time (for example, the FBI broadened its definition of rape in 2013), so long-term comparisons carry caveats.

title: Property crime rate by state
description: Burglary, larceny-theft and motor vehicle theft reported to police, per 100,000 residents.

howToRead: Counts crimes reported to police, not all crimes: many go unreported, especially property crimes and rape.
The FBI changed reporting systems in 2021 and many agencies did not submit that year, so 2021 is the least complete year.
caveats: A state-year is left blank when agencies covering less than 60% of its residents reported (78 blanks).

Rates are computed from the agencies that reported. The FBI's official national estimates fill in for non-reporting agencies and run 1-6% lower in some years (1991: about 758 violent crimes per 100,000 vs. 798 here). Cite "FBI Crime Data Explorer, reported agencies" when using these.
Definitions changed over time (for example, the FBI broadened its definition of rape in 2013), so long-term comparisons carry caveats.

title: Households with broadband by county

unit.label: Share of households with broadband (any type)

description: Share of households with a broadband subscription of any type: cable, fiber, DSL, satellite or a cellular data plan.

source.dataset: American Community Survey 5-year estimates, Table B28002 (2020–2024)

howToRead: Each year is a 5-year average: "2024" covers 2020–2024. Compare periods that don't overlap (2019 vs. 2024) for the clearest trend.
This counts households that pay for or have home internet, not where service is available. A household can lack broadband because of cost or choice, not only because no provider serves it.
caveats: Connecticut replaced its counties with planning regions in 2022, so it appears as no data on the county map.
Survey estimates: small counties have wide margins of error, so differences of a few points there are often noise.
For where service is available (by address and speed), see the FCC National Broadband Map: broadbandmap.fcc.gov.

title: CO₂ emissions per person by country
description: Carbon dioxide emitted from fossil fuels and industry in each country, divided by its population.

source.dataset: CO₂ emissions per capita, based on the Global Carbon Budget

howToRead: Counts emissions where goods are produced, not where they are consumed. Countries that import many goods look cleaner than their consumption implies.
caveats: Excludes emissions from land-use change such as deforestation.

title: Forest cover by country
description: Share of each country's land covered by forest.

source.dataset: World Development Indicators (AG.LND.FRST.ZS), from UN FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment

howToRead: Counts land with trees taller than 5 meters covering more than 10% of the area, including planted forests.
caveats: A country can lose old-growth forest while gaining plantations and show little net change.

title: GDP by country
description: Total value of goods and services produced in each country, converted to U.S. dollars at market exchange rates.

source.dataset: World Development Indicators (NY.GDP.MKTP.CD)

howToRead: Values are in each year's dollars, so everyone grows over time partly because of inflation.
caveats: Market exchange rates understate economies where everyday goods are cheap (China, India). Purchasing-power comparisons tell a different story.
GDP measures the size of an economy, not how well off its people are; divide by population for that.

title: Life expectancy by country
description: How many years a newborn would live if current death rates stayed the same for their whole life.

source.dataset: World Development Indicators (SP.DYN.LE00.IN), from UN Population Division

howToRead: Low life expectancy in the past was driven mostly by child deaths, not people dying at 40.
caveats: It is a snapshot of death rates in a given year, so shocks like COVID-19 dip it temporarily.
